newsitem.title: CHINA: New honours point to Hong Kong's top people.
newsitem.headline: New honours point to Hong Kong's top people.

text.p: North on the political compass of Chinese-ruled Hong Kong was set on Wednesday as 12 residents received its highest honour, the Grand Bauhinia Medal.

Chief Executive Tung Chee-hwa and Chinese Vice-Premier Qian Qichen rewarded people for service to China and Hong Kong, instead of Queen and Empire as Britain's Prince Charles had when he handed out the last knighthoods of the bygone era on Sunday.

Perhaps most indicative of the new political order in Hong Kong was the medal for Henry Fok Ying-tung, a business and real estate tycoon cold-shouldered for decades by the British as a communist sympathiser with mainland China.
Fok broke the U.N. embargo on China during the Korean War and helped broker Chinese participation in a bail-out of Tung's family shipping company in the 1980s.
Former governor Chris Patten was fond of describing Hong Kong as a Chinese success story with distinctly British characteristics.
As he sailed away aboard the royal yacht Britannia, he might have made the same observation of Wednesday's ceremony.
The Grand Bauhinia Medal, a gold medallion embossed with a bauhinia blossom and hung from a red and gold ribbon, seemed to some to copy the Queen's birthday list honours.
The setting, the grand ballroom in Government House, Patten's residence as the 28th and last governor, looked much as it did during his tenure.
Stewards in white tunics draped with elaborate gold and silver braid escorted guests to their seats as a Hong Kong police band played music, just as they had under Patten.
But the national anthem was China's, not Britain's. So, too, was the red flag flying where the Union Jack had hung for 150 years.
And the ceremony was conducted entirely in Chinese, a sure sign Hong Kong is under new management.
"I've been in this room many times in recent years and it's a bit odd to see so many familiar faces but not Patten's," said one British guest.
"There's no doubt about it, Hong Kong is part of China now. Those who succeed in the future here will be those who make the best of the new situation."
Eleven of the medal's 12 recipients on Wednesday were men, mostly elderly, prominent in Hong Kong legal, banking, manufacturing, educational and political circles.
Among them was Lo Tak-shing, a pro-China lawyer and one-time contender for Tung's job as Hong Kong's chief executive, and executive councillor Sir Sze-yuen Chung.
The only woman honoured was veteran pro-Chinese politician Elsie Tu.
